title: Balancing Pipeline Parallelism with Vocabulary Parallelism
problem: In pipeline-parallel LLM training, embedding and output vocabulary layers placed on one pipeline stage cause severe computation and memory imbalance, worsening pipeline bubbles and memory bottlenecks especially for large vocabularies.
motivation: Modern LLMs use large vocabularies (32K-200K tokens) where the embedding and output projection layers require substantial FLOPs and memory. When concentrated on the first/last pipeline stage, this creates imbalance that reduces throughput.
method: Vocabulary Parallelism distributes embedding and output layers (which handle vocabulary processing—the complete set of tokens the model can work with) evenly across pipeline devices instead of concentrating them on one device. The method reduces communication overhead between devices, measured in all-reduce barriers (device synchronization points), through two strategies: Algorithm 1 cuts these from 3 to 2, and Algorithm 2 reduces to 1 by computing softmax outputs online (incrementally rather than storing intermediate values) and using pre-computed gradients. This integrates with existing pipeline scheduling methods like 1F1B and V-Half.
key_novelty: Computing softmax outputs incrementally (online softmax) combined with pre-computed gradients reduces inter-device communication barriers from 3 to 1, enabling vocabulary computation to integrate into existing pipeline schedules with minimal extra memory cost.
contributions: Vocabulary Parallelism: even partition of vocabulary layers across all pipeline stages
Algorithm 2: 1-barrier vocabulary pass via online softmax and pre-computed gradients
Integration framework for VP with 1F1B and V-Half pipeline schedules
Perfect compute and memory balance when combined with V-Half schedule
baselines: Naive pipeline parallelism (vocabulary on one stage)
limitations: Small constant activation memory overhead added; communication pattern more complex; benefit scales with vocabulary size (smaller vocabularies see less gain); requires modification to pipeline scheduling logic.
